title: Two Sensors That Must Agree: A Cross-Check With a Debounce, What It Costs in False Trips and Late Detection, and What It Cannot Catch

questions.question: Two sensors disagree. What does that prove?
options: That the one reading further from the last agreed value is wrong
That both are wrong, since a good pair never disagrees
Nothing, until a third sensor is added
That they are not both right: which one is wrong is not known, and a safe design does not need to know
questions.explanation: The check shows a disagreement and cannot say whose fault it is. The safe response does not depend on knowing: neither is believed.

questions.question: A fault has latched and then the two channels agree again. What is the state?
options: Still faulted: it has shown that it can disagree, and only reset() clears it
ok: the channels agree, so the fault has cleared
suspect, until three good samples in a row
ok, with the value set to the last agreed one
questions.explanation: A pair that disagreed has shown that something is wrong, and agreeing again does not show it has been mended. Someone has to look and reset it.

questions.question: With noise of 0.02 on each channel, how many false trips did a tolerance of 0.04 and no debounce give in 100000 healthy samples?
options: 0: healthy sensors do not disagree
15797: 1.4 sigma of the difference is exceeded once in six samples
questions.explanation: The difference of two noises of 0.02 has a sigma of 0.028, so a tolerance of 0.04 is passed about one sample in six. A debounce of 3 cut it to 303.

questions.question: What does a wider tolerance and a longer debounce cost?
options: Detection time: from 3 samples to 29 in the drift test, and time is stopping distance
Nothing: a quieter check is simply better
Memory for the extra samples
Accuracy of the agreed value
questions.explanation: Every sample the check waits is a sample the robot keeps moving on a bad reading. The most sensitive setting found the drift in 3 samples and the least in 29.

questions.question: Both channels read 1.5 m when the truth is 3.0 m. What does the check say?
options: fault: the value is far from the truth
ok, value 1.5: a common cause failure is invisible to a check between two channels that share it
suspect: both readings changed at once
unknown, since the truth is 3.0 m
questions.explanation: The check compares the channels with each other and has no access to the truth. Two sensors fooled the same way agree perfectly.

questions.question: Why is a check that trips on noise dangerous to safety?
options: It wears out the relay that it trips
It makes the readings noisier
The machine stops for no reason, and the check is switched off, which leaves the machine with none
It slows the control loop
questions.explanation: People do not put up with a machine that stops for nothing. The usual result is that the check is turned off, and then there is no check.
